c.v: A mission moves through five states: idle, running, cancelling, finished and failed. From memory, name the five edges it may follow between them, one line each as
, and say in one sentence why finished and failed have no arrows leaving them. Then write a
function taking the two states and returning whether that edge exists, and run it against a handful of pairs, including at least one that should be refused. Take 10 minutes.
. Finished and failed have no arrows leaving them because a mission that has ended does not resume; whatever comes next is a new mission.

answer.text:
idle        -> running     true
running     -> cancelling  true
cancelling  -> finished    true
running     -> failed      true
running     -> idle        false
finished    -> running     false

c.v: You pass with all five edges named correctly, the reason finished and failed have none leaving them, and a function that agrees with that table on both an accepted and a refused pair. Four of the five edges, or a function untested against a refused pair, is a partial pass. Drawing an edge from finished or failed to anywhere else is a fail: it treats the end of a mission as a state like the others, which is the mistake this topic is about.

State lets an object change what it does when it is called, by changing which state object it currently delegates to, rather than by checking a flag inside every method. The object that changes is the
; each named mode it can be in is a
, given its own class implementing a common interface; the context holds one state at a time, usually through a
to that interface, and every operation the context exposes forwards to it.
The problem is a method whose body is a chain of
checks, repeated in every other method the object has. Adding a state means finding and updating every one of those chains, and forgetting one is a silent bug, not a build error.

The mechanism is that each state's class implements only the operations that state reacts to; an operation a state ignores does nothing by default, so the object stays where it is. A transition is a state's own method returning the next state, which the context installs in place of itself. The context's own code never mentions which state it is in.

What it costs is a class per state, and every transition allocates or moves one, so it earns that cost only when a state's behaviour genuinely differs across several operations. A handful of states with one small rule each, checked in one place, is usually smaller and no less safe as a plain enum and a switch, and the compiler's own unhandled-case warning finds a state you forgot to add.
sit between the two: a closed set of small state values, visited by one function, with the same compile-time check for a missing branch that state classes cannot offer at all.

You meet this wherever a robot or a mission has named modes with real rules about which one follows which, and the interview question is exactly that: draw the states, implement the transitions, and say which of the three shapes earns its keep here.

subs.title: State pattern versus enum and switch versus variant

c.v: moves between three modes, and what each of its operations does depends entirely on which one it is in. One class per state, each overriding only the events it reacts to, is the classic shape:

blocks.text:
start:              disconnected
after connect():    connecting
close() while connecting, ignored: connecting
after open_ack():   connected
after close():      disconnected

c.v: in its own methods; it only calls whichever event the caller raised and installs whatever comes back.
while connecting does nothing, silently, because

, and the base class's default is to ignore it, which is worth noticing before it becomes a bug: a state that should refuse an event still has to say so somehow, which the failure cases below come back to. Gamma, Helm, Johnson and Vlissides describe exactly this shape in the behavioural chapter of the 1994 catalogue (
): an object appears to change its class as its state changes, because every operation is redirected through a state object that can be swapped for another implementing the same interface.

Three states and four events already needed four classes and a base. The trade this pattern makes explicit is the one Klaus Iglberger's Guideline 15 in C++ Software Design names for any class hierarchy: a new state is one new class, written once, and nothing existing has to change; a new operation,

say, has to be added to the base and considered in every state class that exists, whether or not most of them do anything with it. That is the cost side of the ledger this pattern asks you to accept, and it is worth asking, before writing the fifth state class, whether the alternative in the worked example would do the same job for less.
The same three-state connection, written as an enum and a switch, and as a
of empty tag structs visited with one function, both do exactly what the state classes did:

blocks.text:
enum: connecting    variant: connecting    agree: true
enum: connecting    variant: connecting    agree: true
enum: connected     variant: connected     agree: true
enum: disconnected  variant: disconnected  agree: true
sizeof SimpleState: 4, sizeof AnyState: 2

c.v: All three shapes, the state classes above and these two, agree on every step.
costs 2, because its three alternatives hold no data of their own and a
needs only its index besides them. Neither allocates, where every transition among the state classes built a new object on the heap. Mateusz Pusz's
CppCon 2018 talk on replacing dynamic polymorphism with std::variant

works through this exact comparison, a small state machine written both ways, and measures the variant version faster to run and shorter to write, with the trade Iglberger's Guideline 15 already named:
for the variant is one function that a new event has to touch in every branch, the same shape as the switch, while a new state is a new alternative and a new branch in each visitor, not a new file.

Reach for the enum and the switch when the states carry no data of their own and the rules read as one function; reach for a variant when some states need to carry a value the others don't, such as a retry count only

has, which a plain enum cannot express; reach for state classes only once several operations, not one, genuinely differ enough per state to be worth their own class and their own file. Three states and four events, as
has here, sit well inside the range where the switch and the variant are both smaller than the four classes and the base it took to say the same thing.

A state machine is often written as a switch on the event, checked once and reused everywhere, rather than as a switch on the state. Here it costs a mission that has already finished the ability to stay finished:

blocks.text:
before: finished
after a stray start event: running

c.v: Nothing here is undefined behaviour and nothing warns: the switch covers every

has nothing to say, and every branch returns a value of the right type. The bug is a design mistake a warning cannot see, checking half of the pair that decides a transition and ignoring the other half entirely. The state classes and the variant in the exercise cannot make this mistake by construction:
arm of the visitor both live under the current state, so there is no branch left to reach for the wrong one.
A happy-path test never finds this.
, so the bug survives exactly the sequence most tests write first. What catches it is testing every pair, beyond the path a mission is expected to take:

blocks.text:
mismatch: idle       + cancel   -> correct idle       buggy cancelling
mismatch: idle       + complete -> correct idle       buggy finished
mismatch: idle       + fail     -> correct idle       buggy failed
mismatch: cancelling + start    -> correct cancelling buggy running
mismatch: cancelling + fail     -> correct cancelling buggy failed
mismatch: finished   + start    -> correct finished   buggy running
mismatch: finished   + cancel   -> correct finished   buggy cancelling
mismatch: finished   + fail     -> correct finished   buggy failed
mismatch: failed     + start    -> correct failed     buggy running
mismatch: failed     + cancel   -> correct failed     buggy cancelling
mismatch: failed     + complete -> correct failed     buggy finished
checked 20 state-event pairs, 11 mismatches

c.v: Eleven of the twenty pairs disagree, eleven edges the cold check's table never drew that the buggy version accepts anyway. A test suite for a state machine is only as good as the pairs it tries, and the number worth writing down is five valid edges out of twenty possible ones: everything else, fifteen pairs here, is expected to be refused, and a test that only drives the five that should succeed never looks at the fifteen that should not. The exercise's
is what makes that check possible to write in the first place: a version that silently stayed put on a bad event, the way
's default did, gives a test nothing to assert against except the state itself, one pair at a time, instead of one boolean per call.
